title: Solar panel degradation: what to expect and when to replace panels
subtitle: Understanding the gradual loss of output over a panel's 25-year life
excerpt: Solar PV panels degrade slowly every year. A standard crystalline silicon panel loses roughly 0.5% of its rated output annually, giving around 88% of original capacity after 25 years. Knowing what is normal degradation and what signals a fault helps you decide when to investigate a drop in generation.
sourceNotes: NREL (National Renewable Energy Laboratory) study on PV degradation rates, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory; IEC 61215 crystalline silicon module qualification testing; MCS panel warranty guidance.

glossaryTerms.definition: Solar photovoltaic panels that convert sunlight into electricity directly, as distinct from solar thermal collectors that heat water.
The gradual, irreversible reduction in a solar panel's power output over time, caused by light-induced degradation, thermal cycling, and material ageing.
An initial rapid drop in solar panel output in the first few days of operation as the silicon material stabilises under sunlight, typically 1–3% for standard silicon modules.

content.text: A
solar PV

panel does not wear out the way a mechanical part does. It degrades gradually, losing a small fraction of its rated power each year. Standard crystalline silicon panels degrade at around 0.5% per year after the initial
light-induced degradation
period. This is normal
PV degradation
and is factored into the manufacturer's power warranty — most panels are warranted to produce at least 80–87% of rated power at year 25.
Worked example — what to expect over 25 years
A 4 kWp system (10 × 400 W panels) installed in 2024. Assuming 0.5%/year degradation and starting generation of 3,500 kWh/year:
Year 1 (after LID): ~3,430 kWh
Year 10: ~3,270 kWh (~93.5% of year 1)
Year 25: ~2,990 kWh (~87% of year 1)
What is a fault versus what is normal degradation
A gradual decline of 0.5–1% per year is normal. A sudden drop of 5–20% in a single year is a fault, not normal ageing. Common causes of sudden generation loss:
Micro-crack propagation — invisible fractures in the silicon cell that cause open-circuit strings. Shows up as one or more panels reading near-zero output in per-panel monitoring.

Potential-induced degradation (PID) — voltage stress causing charge accumulation at the glass surface, particularly in systems without proper grounding. Can cause 15–25% generation loss but is often reversible with a PID recovery unit.
Delamination — the EVA encapsulant layer separates from the glass, visible as bubbles or yellowing. Typically irreversible.
When to replace panels

Panels rarely need replacing at the end of their 25-year power warranty — the system still generates at 80–87% capacity and replacement makes sense only if the economics of new higher-efficiency panels outweigh the cost and disruption. Replace individual panels when a panel fails a fault test, shows delamination, or has degraded to below 70% of rated capacity while other panels in the string are still above 80%.
Checking generation with year-on-year comparison

Compare generation month-by-month against the same month in the previous year rather than against an absolute target. Weather varies year to year; a year-on-year comparison of the same calendar month controls for irradiance differences better than comparing against an annual average.

rows.symptom: Generation has dropped more than 10% year-on-year
rows.cause: Possible fault: PID, micro-cracks, or a failed DC optimiser or microinverter
rows.fix: Check per-panel monitoring if available; commission a drone thermal survey or a panel IV-curve test to identify underperforming panels.

rows.symptom: Generation lower than expected from year one
rows.cause: Panels were installed with a known LID but the installer modelled pre-LID output; or system is shaded by a new structure
rows.fix: Compare actual output against the MCS prediction document the installer provided; check for new shading sources (tree growth, new building).
